summary: Gives the detailed specifications for NetBIOS over TCP/UDP, including packet formats, protocols, and defined constants and variables. It supports local and internetwork operation and complements RFC 1001, which gives the general concepts and methods.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1002 gives the exact packet formats and procedures for NetBIOS services over TCP and UDP. It complements RFC 1001, which explains the concepts and node roles.

subtitle: Packet formats, procedures, and constants for NetBIOS name, session, and datagram services.

tldr.problem: RFC 1001 describes how NetBIOS services use TCP and UDP, but implementations need exact packet fields, operation codes, and procedures to interoperate.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1002 specifies DNS-style name-service packets, TCP session packets, UDP datagram packets, procedures for node types and servers, and shared constants.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1002 is an Internet Standard and the detailed companion to RFC 1001. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

today: RFC 1002 is an Internet Standard published in March 1987. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; RFC 1001 provides its concepts and methods.

sections.title: What the Detailed Specification Covers
sections.content:
RFC 1002 specifies the packet formats and protocols for NetBIOS over TCP and UDP. It complements RFC 1001, which describes concepts and methods.

The document describes packets for name, session, and datagram services, then gives protocol procedures for B, P, and M nodes and the NetBIOS Name Server. It ends with constants and variables shared by implementations.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC is the implementation-level companion to RFC 1001. It defines the fields, codes, and procedures that let different systems exchange NetBIOS packets.

sections.title: NetBIOS Names on the Wire
sections.content:
Packets for all three services use the compressed domain-name format described in RFC 883. A domain name is encoded as length-prefixed labels and ends with a zero-length root label.

The first label is the 32-character first-level encoding of a 16-byte NetBIOS name. A label length can be at most 63 bytes; name-compression pointers may be used in name-service packets but not session or datagram packets.
sections.plainLanguage: NetBIOS packet names use length-prefixed domain-name labels. Name-service packets can use pointers to reuse an earlier label and save space.

sections.title: Name-Service Packets
sections.content:
Name-service packets follow the DNS packet layout: a header, question entries, and answer, authority, and additional records. The header includes a transaction ID, operation code, flags, result code, and counts for each section.

Operation codes identify queries, registrations, releases, WACK responses, and refreshes. A NetBIOS resource record can identify a name owner and its IP address, as well as whether the name is a group and what node type owns it.

If a UDP response is too large for the 576-byte limit, its truncation flag tells the requester to repeat the query using TCP. A WACK response tells the requester how many seconds to wait before the final response.
sections.plainLanguage: Name-service packets use a DNS-like header and record sections. A transaction ID matches a reply to its request, and a truncation flag tells the client when to retry over TCP.

sections.title: Session Packets
sections.content:
Session packets travel over TCP and begin with a four-byte header: a one-byte type, a one-byte flags field, and a 16-bit length. The length counts bytes after the length field, while one flag bit acts as an additional high-order length bit.

Types identify session messages, requests, positive and negative responses, retarget responses, and keep-alives. A session request carries called and calling names; a retarget response carries an IP address and port. Negative responses include an error code such as called name not present or insufficient resources.
sections.plainLanguage: Each TCP session packet starts with a type, flags, and length. The type tells the receiver whether it is a request, response, data message, redirect, or keep-alive.

sections.title: Datagram Packets
sections.content:
A datagram packet begins with a 14-byte header containing its type, flags, identifier, source IP address and port, total datagram length, and fragment offset. The type distinguishes direct-to-unique, direct-to-group, broadcast, error, and query messages.

Fragmentation flags indicate whether more data follows and whether this is the first fragment. Data packets then carry the source name, destination name, and user data. Error packets identify problems such as a missing destination name or invalid name format.
sections.plainLanguage: The datagram header identifies the message, sender, size, and fragment position. The packet then carries names and user data, or an error or relay query.

sections.title: Node and Server Procedures
sections.content:
The RFC gives pseudo-code for how B, P, and M nodes register, find, and release names. B nodes broadcast on their local network; P nodes ask the NBNS; M nodes broadcast first and use the NBNS if needed. Requests are retried when responses do not arrive.

The NBNS may check whether an existing owner still holds a name. A non-secured server can ask the registering node to challenge the owner; a secured server performs the challenge itself. A response or silence determines whether the name can be registered.

Session procedures discover a name, open TCP, and process acceptance, rejection, or retargeting. Datagram procedures let P and M nodes ask an NBDD whether it will relay a group or broadcast packet; if not, they can request the owner list from the NBNS.
sections.plainLanguage: Each node type follows its own steps for name lookup and registration. The NBNS can check an old name owner, and an NBDD can relay group or broadcast datagrams.

sections.title: Ports and Timing Defaults
sections.content:
The name service uses port 137 over UDP and TCP, the datagram service uses port 138 over UDP, and the session service uses port 139 over TCP.

The default maximum datagram length is 576 bytes. Broadcast requests retry after 250 milliseconds, up to 3 attempts; unicast requests retry after 5 seconds, up to 3 attempts. The session service allows 4 connection attempts by default and uses a 30-second close timeout; a 60-second keep-alive is recommended.
sections.plainLanguage: The three services use separate ports for name lookup, datagrams, and TCP sessions. The RFC also sets default retry, packet-size, and session timing values.

fields.name: FLAGS
fields.desc: Includes the extra high-order length bit.

fields.name: LENGTH
fields.desc: Counts bytes following the length field.

items.label: SESSION REQUEST
items.desc: Starts a session and names both parties.

items.label: NEGATIVE RESPONSE
items.desc: Rejects the session with an error code.

items.label: RETARGET RESPONSE
items.desc: Gives a different IP address and port.

items.label: SESSION KEEP ALIVE
items.desc: Checks the session path when configured.
